part_title: AWS Console, CLI and SDK: Identity, Credentials and API Access

scenes.title: Console, CLI and SDK access
scenes.narration: The central message in this slide is that three interfaces—the AWS Console, AWS CLI and AWS SDK—invoke the same underlying AWS service APIs. The difference is how the user or workload supplies credentials and builds requests. For a human employee, IAM Identity Center is a preferred workforce sign-in path and can provide short-lived sessions. For an application on EC2, ECS or Lambda, an attached IAM role supplies temporary credentials without placing static secrets in application code. The lower panel illustrates a credential provider chain, including environment variables, shared profiles, configured Identity Center sessions, compute-role providers and other supported sources. The exact ordering differs by SDK and configuration, so do not assume the diagram is a universal sequence for every language. Avoid embedding long-lived access keys into source files or container images. When debugging an AccessDenied, first identify the actual calling principal, then check the action, resource and applicable policies. Authentication proves which identity made the request; authorisation determines what it may do.

scenes.title: CLI versus SDK: Automate or Build
scenes.narration: This side-by-side code example compares a terminal command with Python boto3. On the left, aws sts get-caller-identity returns the effective caller's account and ARN, with the Region set in the CLI invocation. On the right, a boto3 Session creates an STS client and calls get_caller_identity to obtain equivalent information inside application code. Both use SDK or CLI credential resolution from the configured environment and profile, and both make signed HTTPS API requests. This is a useful first check when a deployment seems to be operating in the wrong account: verify the caller before applying changes. The lower comparison includes Region selection, automatic retry behavior and errors. Retries help with transient throttling or network issues, but programs must still handle exceptions and avoid repeating non-idempotent actions blindly. Pick the CLI for quick administration and shell automation; pick an SDK when the API operation belongs inside application logic with richer error handling and types. Neither interface grants permissions beyond the active identity's IAM policies.
